# What each layer sees

A three-layer convolutional net taught **one layer at a time, with no labels anywhere**.
Layer 1 looks at pixels. Layer 2 looks at what layer 1 said. Layer 3 looks at what layer 2
said. Each is trained by the same rule — *fire rarely, and disagree with your neighbours* —
and each is frozen before the next one starts.

Then the network is run backwards: pick a unit, start from noise, and push the picture
uphill until that unit is as excited as it can be. What comes back is a picture of what
that unit is looking for, generated from the weights themselves.

**The point is what changes down the rows.** Layer 1 wants a bar about eleven pixels
across. Layer 2 wants a patch of oriented texture about twenty-six across. Layer 3 wants a
structured region about sixty across. Nobody designed that ladder — it is what falls out of
stacking the same rule three times, and it is the reason convolutional nets are built deep
rather than wide.

## Why the first layer's dream is boring, and why that matters

Run it and look at the top row: mostly a small bar, and at the default settings often just
a saturated block.

A single convolution is **linear**. Gradient ascent on a linear function has no interior
maximum — there is no *best* input, only a direction to keep going in, so the picture runs
to the clamp and stops. The dream tells you nothing because there is nothing to tell.

Put a **ReLU** in and stack a second convolution, and suddenly there is something to find:
a layer-2 unit responds to a *combination* of layer-1 features, and combinations have best
cases. That is the entire argument for nonlinearity, and it is visible here as the
difference between row one and row two.

Delete the ReLU nodes and run it again. Two convolutions with nothing between them collapse
into a single convolution, and the ladder collapses with them.

## The settings that make this legible

Two of the Deep Dream widgets are doing almost all the work, and the defaults are wrong for
this job.

**`objective` is set to `max`, not `mean`.** Maximising the mean over the whole feature map
asks "what image makes this filter fire *everywhere*", and the answer is always the cheapest
tileable texture — every layer comes back as diagonal hatching and the depth is invisible.
`max` asks what a *single unit* wants, which is the question feature visualisation is
supposed to be asking, and the answer is a feature sitting on a blank field.

**`smoothness` is 0.4, not 0.**  Left at zero, ascent discovers that the cheapest way to
excite an edge detector is a one-pixel grating, and the result is corduroy.

**`size` is 96, deliberately small.** The receptive field of layer 3 is about sixty pixels.
On a big canvas that feature is a speck; on a small one it fills the frame.

Turn `objective` back to `mean` and re-run for the before-and-after — it is the single most
dramatic knob here.

## Chaining the training

Three **Discover Kernels** nodes in a row, each naming the layer below it in `layer`.

Naming a layer does two things at once, and both are needed. The optimiser is handed *only*
that layer's weights, so nothing below moves — measured drift is exactly 0.00. And the loss
is computed on *that layer's* output rather than the model's, so the layer is judged on its
own responses instead of on how well it serves the layers above.

Freeze without moving the loss and you have end-to-end training with one layer unlocked.
Move the loss without freezing and the objective simply rewrites the layers below to make
its own job easier. Neither is what "train a layer" means.

Measured on the portrait: layer 1 improves sparsity 0.253 on its untrained floor, layer 2
improves 0.199, layer 3 improves 0.064 — **the gains shrink**, and by layer 3 the kernels
also start repeating each other (overlap 0.43). Three layers is about where this stops
paying at this size, which is worth knowing before adding a fourth.
